description: We are a team from Brazil, passionate about technology and innovation. We love developing games and are ready to combine our creativity, programming, and design skills to create incredible experiences in this challenge!
summary:
We developed an educational 2D game that teaches children aged 7 to 12 about Mars and astronomy. The player leads a team of astronauts at a base on the Martian surface. They complete missions, go on expeditions and keep four essential resources in balance: life support, base shielding, food and water, and energy.

The game is built on real NASA data. Through the DONKI API, events catalogued by NASA, such as solar storms reaching Mars, become challenges the player has to face. Data from the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) becomes the resources they must manage. Scientific information shapes every decision in the game.

This matters because children often learn about science by memorizing it, which makes it feel distant and dull. Our game lets them experience space science through play. All the drawings were done by hand, giving the game a unique visual identity that captures children's attention.
details:
Benefits and intended impact
Astronomy is often taught through memorization, which makes it feel distant to children. Our game lets them learn by doing: they see how space weather affects a mission and why resources matter for survival. We want to spark curiosity about space science early, helping children see science as something exciting and within their reach, which may also inspire future careers in STEM.

Tools and technologies
The game was developed with GameMaker using GameMaker Language (GML). NASA data is fetched through the DONKI API, and we used Postman to test the API routes and check the responses before integrating them into the game. We also used Claude, an AI assistant, to support development, helping with coding, debugging and organizing ideas. The artwork was hand-drawn in Aseprite.

Creativity
Instead of presenting data as charts or text, we turned real scientific records into gameplay. NASA’s events become challenges and its research data becomes resources. All animations were hand-drawn by the team, giving the game a unique and consistent art style made for young players.

Factors we considered
We designed for our target age: simple controls, clear visual feedback and short text so younger children can play without help. We balanced difficulty to keep the game challenging but not frustrating. We also kept the scientific content accurate while making it easy to understand.
